findings.paper_title: Appendix 4b - Transfers to and from reserves 25.26
findings.headline: Insurance claim excess for Mount Pavilion lead replacement indicates aging asset liabilities
findings.detail: The Insurance and Legal Reserve includes a specific drawdown to cover an insurance claim excess (£9,960) for lead replacement at Mount Pavilion. This signals environmental and health hazards in council-owned buildings that are triggering insurance claims.
findings.matters: Environmental remediation (lead removal) is a material liability. If Mount Pavilion requires lead replacement, other council buildings may have similar exposure, adding to future capital demands.
findings.figures: Insurance Claim Excess for the Mount Pavilion - Lead Replacement (9,960)
findings.quote: Insurance Claim Excess for the Mount Pavilion - Lead Replacement 0 (10,000) 0 (10,000) (9,960) (9,960)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4b - Transfers to and from reserves 25.26
findings.headline: Leisure centre reprocurement procurement timeline is slipping; £2m commitment to new operator remains
findings.detail: The council is preparing to hand over leisure centres to a new operator with a £2m investment fund planned for 2026/27. However, planned releases of procurement funding (legal, SLC, project management totalling £71.5k) did not occur in full — only the legal element (£58,178 of £20k planned) was spent, while SLC and PM releases dropped to zero. This suggests delays in the reprocurement process.
findings.matters: A delayed leisure service transition is a material change in council operations and potentially service quality. The £2m new investment is significant; delays may signal problems with the market or the proposed arrangement.
findings.figures: Release of funds to support Leisure Centre reprocurement: SLC planned (29,530) actual 0; Legal planned (20,000) actual (58,178); PM planned (22,500) actual 0. Investment fund to new operator: (15,000)
findings.quote: Release of funds to support Leisure Centre reprocurement 07/05/2024 PH - SLC 0 (29,530) 0 (29,530) 0

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4b - Transfers to and from reserves 25.26
findings.headline: General Fund Balance reduced by 45%, from £3.75m to £2.05m
findings.detail: The General Fund Balances fell from an opening of £3,749,514 to a closing of £2,049,514, a reduction of £1.7m. While this transfer appears planned (it's identical in both estimate and outturn columns), the scale of the reduction cuts the unallocated buffer by nearly half.
findings.matters: A falling general fund balance reduces the council's financial headroom and flexibility to absorb future shocks. Lenders assess this as a key liquidity and financial resilience measure.
findings.figures: General Fund Balances: opening £3,749,514, closing £2,049,514

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4b - Transfers to and from reserves 25.26
findings.headline: £600k of legal cases provision funded from the Insurance and Legal Reserve
findings.detail: The Insurance and Legal Reserve drew down £659k in total outturn, vs £59k estimated. The variance of £600k is attributed to funding legal cases — significantly more than planned at the start of the year. This indicates material legal exposure that materialised during the year and had to be paid from reserves.
findings.matters: A sudden £600k legal liability is a material stress on the council's position. Lenders would need to understand what these cases involve and whether they represent isolated incidents or systemic issues.
findings.figures: Insurance and Legal Reserve outturn expenditure (659,170) vs estimate (59,220); line item 'To fund legal cases provision 0 (600,000)'
findings.quote: To fund legal cases provision 0 (600,000) (600,000)

findings.paper_title: 20260505 Audit and Standards Committe report pre audit
findings.headline: Audit disclaimed opinion will continue for at least another year due to sector-wide audit delays
findings.detail: The council's 2024/25 accounts received a disclaimed opinion when signed off in February 2026 under 'backstop' arrangements due to audit delays affecting the whole sector. The 2025/26 accounts are expected to follow the same path, with formal sign-off expected November 2026 or soon after, meaning the accounts will not carry an audit opinion confirming they present a true and fair view.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the auditor could not reach a conclusion about whether the accounts present a true and fair view; this creates material uncertainty about reported financial position and is highly relevant to lenders assessing creditworthiness and reserve adequacy
findings.figures: 2024/25 signed off February 2026; 2025/26 expected November 2026
findings.quote: Owing to the well documented and reported audit delays across the sector, the council's 2024/25 accounts were signed off under the so-called 'backstop' arrangements in February 2026, with a disclaimed opinion. This was a standard part of the 'backstop' arrangements but it means that the council will be subject to a disclaimed opinion on the accounts for at least another year.

findings.headline: Council's reserves increased 10% to £44.5m while maintaining £10.7m unfinanced capital requirement
findings.detail: Reserves grew from £40,299k to £44,456k (increase of £4,157k) while the council had a £10,709k unfinanced capital financing requirement and chose not to borrow externally. The council is accumulating cash reserves while leaving capital needs unfunded.
findings.matters: Reserve trajectory signals financial strategy and confidence. Building liquidity while not borrowing suggests either prudent caution in an uncertain environment or deliberate accumulation for contingencies. A lender needs to understand reserve adequacy and sustainability of this approach.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure was 27% below budget with no explanation in the outturn
findings.detail: Capital spending in 2025/26 was £18,933k against a budget of £26,063k—a variance of £7,130k (27%). All actual expenditure was financed in-year with no unfinanced capital expenditure. The report provides no commentary on the cause of the significant underspend.
findings.matters: Large planned-vs-actual variances signal either unrealistic planning, service delivery challenges, or unannounced changes in strategy. A lender needs confidence the council can deliver on its capital plans.
findings.figures: Budget £26,063k, Actual £18,933k, Variance £7,130k (27% underspend)
findings.quote: The table below shows the actual capital expenditure and how this was financed: Capital expenditure [2025/26 Budget] 26,063 [2025/26 Actual] 18,933

findings.headline: Council temporarily breached its approved counterparty investment limits on four occasions in 2025/26
findings.detail: During the year the council exceeded its approved counterparty limits (controls that restrict credit exposure to individual institutions) four times. All breaches were short-term and resolved promptly with minimal financial losses. The council states controls remain in place to prevent recurrence.
findings.matters: Counterparty limits are fundamental credit risk controls. Four breaches in a single year—even if temporary—indicate either inadequate limit-setting or operational control slippage. A lender wants assurance the council's risk framework is working.
findings.figures: Four breach occasions in one financial year; minimal financial losses
findings.quote: During the year, there were four occasions where the council temporarily breached these approved limits. The breaches were all short-term, identified promptly and resolved quickly, with minimal financial losses incurred, and controls remain in place to minimise the risk recurrence.

findings.headline: Wyre did not undertake any external borrowing during 2025/26 despite a £10.7m capital financing requirement
findings.detail: The council managed its entire capital financing need (CFR £10,709k) through internal resources—reserves, balances, and cash flow—rather than accessing external debt markets. This was a deliberate strategy to avoid long-term borrowing at rates above 5%, based on the expectation that borrowing costs will fall through 2026-27.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can access debt markets or is choosing to avoid it. Not borrowing against a £10.7m capital need while building reserves signals either strong liquidity/prudence or potential constraints on market access.
findings.figures: CFR £10,709k, external borrowing £0k, reserves increased to £44,456k
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the Authority did not undertake any external borrowing. This meant that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), was managed entirely using internal resources, including reserves, balances and cash flow.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget, Council Tax and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Identified building maintenance backlog of £5.5m with funding uncertain
findings.detail: Building condition surveys in 2024 identified approximately £5.5m of works needed on key assets. The council acknowledges 'there is likely to be a requirement for additional fund to made available prior to year five if all work is undertaken'. Funding is to come from capital receipts and Asset Management Reserve; the report notes the council will need further asset disposals to generate necessary capital receipts.
findings.matters: Deferred maintenance typically becomes more expensive to remedy. The council's ability to fund these works is constrained and depends on selling assets, which is not sustainable long-term. Backlog indicates underinvestment in estate.
findings.figures: £5.5m identified maintenance works; projected Capital Receipts balance £892,882 at 31 March 2026; Asset Management Reserve at £2.9m
findings.quote: The current estimate for all works identified on key assets is in the region of £5.5m

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget, Council Tax and Capital Programme
findings.headline: CIPFA financial resilience index flags fees and charges as high-risk
findings.detail: The 2024/25 CIPFA financial resilience index shows all of Wyre's indicators as low-risk except the ratio of 'Fees and Charges to Service Expenditure', which is high-risk. The council acknowledges this needs monitoring and identifies it explicitly as 'an area for review in order to bridge the budget gap'.
findings.matters: The council is dependent on discretionary income (fees and charges) to fund services. High-risk flagging means this income is vulnerable—if demand falls or the council must freeze charges, revenue will suffer. The council already plans to use income increases to close the budget gap.
findings.figures: High-risk CIPFA rating for Fees and Charges to Service Expenditure ratio
findings.quote: All of Wyre's initial 2024/25 results for our family group are low-risk apart from our ratio of Fees and Charges to Service Expenditure

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget, Council Tax and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Audit sign-offs under backstop arrangements, not full opinions
findings.detail: The 2023/24 accounts were 'signed off under the backstop arrangements' and the 2024/25 accounts are expected to be similarly signed off. The report notes this will 'conclude prior to local government reorganisation' — indicating a multi-year audit difficulty. Backstop arrangements are a fallback when an auditor cannot give a full audit opinion.
findings.matters: Backstop sign-offs signal auditor concerns about the authority's accounts or controls that prevent full assurance. A lender would flag this as a governance risk and question what underlying issues drove the need for backstop arrangements.
findings.figures: Two consecutive years: 2023/24 and 2024/25 accounts signed under backstop
findings.quote: The 2023/24 accounts have now been signed off under the backstop arrangements with no material changes to the draft version

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget, Council Tax and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Waste collection relies on unguaranteed and delayed EPR packaging funding
findings.detail: The council was promised Extended Producer Responsibility packaging grant of £1.363m for 2025/26, revised to £1.395m for 2026/27 forward, but 'at the time of writing no monies had been received'. Future payments are 'not guaranteed' and will trigger efficiency assessments from an unspecified date between April 2026 and 2028. The council budgets to use the full assumed allocation to offset estimated waste collection costs of over £1.7m annually (for food waste collection alone).
findings.matters: The council is financing core service costs (waste collection) from unguaranteed grant funding that has already been delayed. If EPR is withdrawn or reduced after 2026, waste budgets will overspend significantly and reserves will need to cover the gap.
findings.figures: £1.395m assumed EPR allocation for 2026/27; over £1.7m annual food waste collection costs; originally promised £995,000 for 2025/26, revised to £1.363m
findings.quote: payments were delayed by central government and at the time of writing no monies had been received. As a Waste Collection Authority, the payment covers estimated net efficient costs associated with collection of household packaging waste from kerbside and communal collections

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget, Council Tax and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Loss of business rates pooling removes £2.5m income source accumulated over three years
findings.detail: The Lancashire 50% Business Rates Retention Pool ends 31 March 2026 after generating £2.5m of additional income between 2022/23 and 2024/25. The council ended pooling due to late/incomplete information from government on redesigned scheme, low likelihood of business rates growth in 2026/27, and raised safety net protection reducing pooling incentive.
findings.matters: This removes a material income stream that had been helping bridge the budget gap. The council relied on business rates growth to close a structural deficit; losing both the pooling income and the prospect of growth worsens the underlying position.
findings.figures: £2.5m total pooling income 2022/23–2024/25; safety net raised to 100% for 2026/27 only
findings.quote: the Lancashire Business Rates 50% Pool comes to an end at 31 March 2026

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget, Council Tax and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Fair funding reforms will cut the council's income by £1.1m over three years
findings.detail: The government's new fair funding formula delivers a structural reduction in grant funding across 2026–29. Wyre faces this alongside declining cash settlements: Revenue Support Grant falls from £4.713m (2026/27) to £3.570m (2028/29). Shire districts nationally see an average 6.42% reduction in this period.
findings.matters: This is not a one-off pressure. The funding reduction is permanent and built into the baseline, forcing the council to find permanent savings or continuously draw reserves. The council already struggles to balance without reserves.
findings.figures: £1.1m cumulative loss 2025/26 to 2028/29; Revenue Support Grant declining £0.556m and then £0.587m in successive years
findings.quote: in cash terms our forecast fair funding reduces and the decline is illustrated over the three years culminating in a cumulative £1.1m loss between 2025/26 and 2028/29

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget, Council Tax and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Council is drawing down reserves unsustainably to balance an underlying budget deficit
findings.detail: The Budget Equalisation Reserve is being drawn down each year with no prospect of recovery. Required draws grow from £2.2m in 2026/27 to £4.7m by 2030/31. The S151 officer explicitly states this reliance on reserves 'is not sustainable', yet forecasts show continuing and accelerating deficits across the MTFP period.
findings.matters: A lender would see a council whose actual operating expenditure exceeds its recurring income, with the gap widening. Once reserves are exhausted, the council cannot balance its budget without service cuts or borrowing.
findings.quote: the continued use of reserves is not sustainable

findings.headline: Council has decided against using government-permitted flexibility to convert capital receipts into revenue funding, suggesting capital pressures are seen as more urgent than revenue ones
findings.detail: Central government allows councils to use capital receipts for revenue purposes, but Wyre has no intention to do so because of the significant schedule of maintenance and capital works required. This indicates capital backlog is the immediate priority.
findings.matters: The decision to prioritise capital spending suggests either significant asset maintenance backlog, or that the council is not deploying available tools to address revenue pressures
findings.figures: No capital receipts strategy approved
findings.quote: At the present time, there is no intention to make use of this flexibility owing to the significant schedule of works required to maintain and invest in our assets and as such no Strategy has yet been approved by Council.

findings.headline: Council has acquired Garstang Swimming Pool from Lancashire County Council, taking on a new operational asset with ongoing maintenance costs
findings.detail: During 2025/26 the council acquired the swimming pool and also a land strip for the new Food Waste Collection Service launching in 2026/27. These are new operational commitments that bring asset maintenance obligations.
findings.matters: New operational assets increase ongoing revenue costs and maintenance liabilities; leisure facilities carry particular risk if usage or income declines
findings.figures: Garstang Swimming Pool acquisition value not specified
findings.quote: Acquisition – During 2025/26 we have acquired Garstang Swimming Pool from Lancashire County Council and a strip of land adjacent to Copse Road Depot, Fleetwood to support the delivery of the new Food Waste Collection Service in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Council capital planning is proceeding amid unresolved uncertainty about local government reorganisation and the council's future structure
findings.detail: The council is explicitly planning capital investment to 'secure the legacy' of the council while awaiting clarity on LGR timescales. This suggests significant uncertainty about the council's future form, responsibilities, and ability to deliver multi-year capital commitments.
findings.matters: LGR could fundamentally alter the council's structure, absorb it into a larger authority, or change its financial obligations, making medium-term capital plans and debt commitments uncertain
findings.figures: No timescale given for LGR resolution
findings.quote: During 2026/27 further work will continue, hopefully in the context of more certainty over Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) and its timescales. As we navigate the future of Wyre and where it sits in the LGR landscape, we will seek to secure the legacy of this council and its ambitions for the borough through capital investment.

findings.headline: The capital programme relies on external funding for over 90% of its value, creating vulnerability if grant priorities or availability change
findings.detail: Much of Wyre's external funding comes from specific sources like Environment Agency sea defences funding, Better Care Fund grants, and UK Shared Prosperity Funding. If these funding streams reduce or redirect, the council has limited internal resources to bridge the gap.
findings.matters: High dependency on grant funding creates execution risk for capital plans and means the council cannot easily pivot if external funding dries up
findings.figures: External funding over 90% of total capital programme
findings.quote: Wyre's Capital Programme has always relied heavily on external funding owing to limited internal resources and a desire not to externally borrow. The council has external funding levels of over 90% (estimated 2025/26 position) of the total capital programme.

findings.headline: Central government funding cuts have created a significant revenue gap that limits the council's ability to fund capital investment from reserves
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that due to funding cuts and a significant gap in ongoing revenue estimates, there is limited scope to contribute from earmarked reserves to capital projects without identifying compensating savings. This severely constrains financial flexibility.
findings.matters: A council facing a revenue deficit has limited financial headroom and cannot easily plug capital shortfalls if external grant funding reduces or projects overrun
findings.figures: 90% of capital programme externally funded (estimated 2025/26)
findings.quote: As a result of central government funding cuts and a significant gap to bridge in our ongoing revenue estimates, there is limited scope for the council to contribute monies from earmarked reserves and general balances without additional compensating savings being identified.

findings.headline: No forecast of cashable efficiencies beyond 2026/27 due to local government reorganisation uncertainty
findings.detail: The council explicitly states 'no future years' cashable efficiencies beyond 2026/27 are included in this year's statement' due to LGR. Efficiencies of £535,360 are forecast for 2026/27 (60% from pension contribution reduction alone), but there are no planned savings for 2027/28 onwards, despite budgets remaining under pressure.
findings.matters: The council has no planned efficiency programme to address the structural funding gap from 2027/28 onwards. This means the gap must be closed entirely by council tax, reserve drawdown, or service cuts. This is a key sustainability gap in the forecast.
findings.figures: Forecast efficiency savings 2026/27: £535,360. Forecast savings 2027/28-2030/31: £0
findings.quote: As a result of forthcoming local government reorganisation, no future years' cashable efficiencies beyond 2026/27 are included in this year's statement.

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation scheduled for April 2028 has no dedicated budget provision despite acknowledged complexity and additional pressures
findings.detail: The council notes LGR is 'on the horizon' with vesting day potentially 1 April 2028. It will 'bring additional pressures and complexities' and there is a need to 'prepare for collaboration, integration and shared capability'. However, the plan explicitly states no funds have been set aside for LGR implementation costs.
findings.matters: A structural reorganisation of local government in 2028 (16 months into this MTFP) will incur costs: system integration, data migration, staff transition, duplicate running costs during merger. Planning for this without a budget provision is a material governance risk and increases the chance of unbudgeted overspends or emergency reserve draws.
findings.figures: LGR vesting day: 1 April 2028
findings.quote: As yet, pending the decision from Central Government in the summer of 2026, no specific funds have been set aside for LGR.

findings.headline: Significant pension contribution cost savings (£318,000 in 2026/27) depend on the triennial pension review assumption dropping from 13.5% to 11%
findings.detail: The MTFP assumes pension contributions for future service costs will fall from the current 13.5% to 11% starting in 2026/27. This generates £318,000 in savings in 2026/27 and rising to £358,000 by 2030/31. The document notes the 2026/27 pay award is not yet agreed.
findings.matters: Pension contribution rates are set by actuarial valuations and can move in either direction. If the triennial review in 2026/27 does not deliver the assumed reduction, the council loses these assumed savings (10% of the 2026/27 efficiency forecast). This is a key budget risk.
findings.figures: Assumed pension savings: £318,000 in 2026/27 rising to £358,000 in 2030/31. Current rate 13.5%, assumed rate 11%
findings.quote: Our pension contribution for future service costs is currently set at 13.5% and 11% has been assumed to be ongoing for the duration of the MTFP generating a saving of £338,000 in 2027/28 rising to £358,000 in 2030/31.

findings.headline: Balanced budgets rely on continuous drawdown of the Budget Equalisation Reserve with accelerating pressures in final years
findings.detail: The council is balancing budgets by using the Budget Equalisation Reserve, with drawdowns of £2.2m in 2026/27, increasing to £4.7m in 2030/31. The document notes pressures on reserves in the final year despite £10m+ of total reserves remaining.
findings.matters: Reserve-funded budgeting is unsustainable long-term. It signals the underlying budget is structurally unbalanced. Accelerating drawdowns in the latter years indicate worsening budget gaps that current assumptions (council tax rises, efficiencies) do not fully solve.
findings.figures: Budget Equalisation Reserve drawdowns: £2.2m (2026/27) to £4.7m (2030/31). Total usable reserves: over £10m
findings.quote: the council will be able to set a balanced budget by utilising the Budget Equalisation Reserve up to 2030/31... pressures on this reserve and others are evident although in aggregate usable un-ringfenced reserves remain of over £10m.

findings.headline: Treasury income forecast to fall by 47% over the MTFP period as interest rates and investment balances decline
findings.detail: Investment income is predicted to halve from just under £750,000 in 2027/28 to less than £400,000 by 2030/31. This income stream is available for budget support but is volatile and declining across the forecast period.
findings.matters: Treasury income volatility limits financial flexibility and predictability. A council losing £350,000 of annual investment income has fewer options to absorb shocks or unplanned costs.
findings.figures: Treasury income 2027/28: just under £750,000; by end of MTFP: less than £400,000
findings.quote: Income from treasury management is predicted to reduce over the MTFP period as interest rates and balances available to invest reduce. Income in 2027/28 is expected to be just under £750,000 dropping to less than £400,000 by the end of the MTFP period.

findings.headline: Core funding loss of £1.1m over the MTFP period with no compensating service reductions
findings.detail: The council's core funding (government grant) is forecast to reduce from £8.9m in 2025/26 to £7.8m in 2028/29. The document states the council is committed to maintaining vital services such as homelessness and refuse collection, and also investing in Council Plan projects, despite this significant funding reduction.
findings.matters: A 12% reduction in core funding over three years forces budget choices. Either services are cut, council tax rises sharply, or reserves are drawn down. The plan opts for the latter, which has finite sustainability.
findings.figures: Core funding: over £8.9m in 2025/26 to just over £7.8m in 2028/29 (£1.1m loss)
findings.quote: Wyre Council's core funding will reduce from over £8.9m in 2025/26 to a forecast figure of just over £7.8m in 2028/29 based on the multi-year settlement (£1.1m loss).

findings.headline: Second consecutive disclaimed audit opinion on annual accounts
findings.detail: The council's 2023/24 accounts received a disclaimed audit opinion under backstop arrangements in February 2025. The 2024/25 accounts will receive the same treatment. A disclaimed opinion means the auditor could not obtain sufficient evidence to conclude whether the accounts present a true and fair view, indicating significant audit concerns.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion is a serious governance weakness that undermines confidence in the council's financial position. For lenders, it complicates creditworthiness assessment; for finance directors, it signals audit control weaknesses.
findings.figures: 2023/24 disclaimed opinion February 2025; 2024/25 expected under same backstop arrangements
findings.quote: the council's 2023/24 accounts were signed off under the so-called 'backstop' arrangements in February 2025, with a disclaimed opinion. This was a standard part of the 'backstop' arrangements, but it means that the council is likely to be subject to disclaimed opinions on the accounts for at least another year.

findings.headline: Budget forecasting volatility: planned deficit of £553k became a £2.2m projected gap before reversing to surplus
findings.detail: The council's 2024-25 budget forecast shifted materially during the year: initial approved deficit of £695k, revised to £553k after final settlement, then escalated to a forecast £2,244k deficit in the November MTFP update before ultimately recording a £19,283m outturn position with no General Fund drawdown required. This volatility suggests forecasting challenges or late-emerging pressures.
findings.matters: Budget forecast accuracy is a key marker of financial control and planning capability. Swings of this magnitude suggest either forecasting weakness or material unplanned cost/income movements that materialised late in the year.
findings.figures: Planned deficit £695k, revised to £553k, forecast £2,244k, actual outturn with 'Increased Spending/Reduced Income' of £844k offset by 'Reduced Spending/Increased Income' of £3,350k
findings.quote: The Council planned a (£695k) deficit in 2024/25 as per the approved budget of £16,663k… later revised to (£553k) when the final settlement figures were published. This was revised to a forecast budget gap of (£2,244k) largely owing to revenue slippage carried forward at year end, as per the November 2024 MTFP update… This was reversed with no drawdown of General Fund reserves required due to an outturn position of £19,283k as at year end.

findings.headline: Council lacks a formal efficiency programme with defined targets, creating reliance on reserves to bridge budget gaps
findings.detail: The council does not have a formal efficiency programme stating a target as a percentage of prior-year expenditure and setting out the efficiency schemes by which savings will be achieved. The auditors raised this as a performance improvement observation (PIO) in 2023-24 and it remains outstanding in 2024-25. The auditors note this demonstrates 'emerging need' for such a programme as the council increasingly relies on General Fund to bridge budget shortfalls.
findings.matters: Councils facing sustained funding pressure need explicit efficiency targets and delivery plans. The absence of a formal programme suggests reactive rather than proactive cost management and increases the risk that expected efficiencies will not be realised.
findings.figures: Efficiency programme document presented for 2024-25 budget anticipated efficiencies of £143,300; original planned deficit £695k, revised to £553k, then forecast gap of £2,244k
findings.quote: However, there is not currently an efficiency programme in place which states a target as a percentage of the previous year's expenditure and sets out the efficiency schemes by which the efficiency savings will be achieved. Although the Council have sufficient reserves to prevent the use of them leading to a financial sustainability risk, this further demonstrates the emerging need for a formal efficiency programme.

findings.headline: General Fund balance contracted sharply from £17m to £4m despite increase in overall reserves
findings.detail: The General Fund (the most liquid and flexible reserve) dropped 76% year-on-year from £17m to £4m. While the council attributes this to a reorganisation of how earmarked reserves are utilised (which increased from £20m to £37m), the General Fund now represents only 9% of what it was, creating concentration risk in less-flexible earmarked reserves.
findings.matters: Lenders track General Fund balance as an indicator of cash flexibility. A sharp decline suggests reduced ability to manage unexpected cost pressures or income shortfalls without dipping into restricted reserves.
findings.figures: General Fund balance 2023-24: £17m; 2024-25: £4m. Earmarked reserves 2023-24: £20m; 2024-25: £37m. Total usable reserves 2023-24: £39.265m; 2024-25: £42.857m
findings.quote: The General Fund balance decreased from £17m in 2023-24 to £4m in 2024-25, however this reflects a reorganisation of how earmarked reserves are utilised.

findings.headline: Auditors issuing disclaimer of opinion on the financial statements due to insufficient audit evidence
findings.detail: KPMG will issue a disclaimer of opinion on 27 February 2026 because they could not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to form an opinion on the financial statements ahead of the Backstop Date. The reason for the disclaimer is described as 'still being finalised with our Department of Professional Practice – Accounting and Reporting team', with a verbal update promised to the Committee.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion means the auditors cannot certify the financial statements are accurate and fairly presented. This significantly undermines reliance on the council's reported financial position and would be a material concern for any lender.
findings.figures: Financial statements covering the year ended 31 March 2025; disclaimer issued 27 February 2026
findings.quote: We will issue a disclaimer of opinion on the Council's financial statements on 27 February 2026. This is because we have been unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over a number of areas of the financial statements as we have been unable to perform the procedures that we consider necessary to form our opinion on the financial statements ahead of the Backstop Date.

findings.headline: Budget process lacks documented evidence of stakeholder engagement: finance-budget holder meetings not logged or tracked.
findings.detail: Meetings between budget holders and finance business partners during budget setting are not formally recorded or tracked. The Council cannot evidence stakeholder involvement in budget development. Management has committed to developing a proforma for budget changes to be reviewed and signed off, but this is scheduled for the 2026/27 cycle.
findings.matters: Lack of documented engagement reduces transparency and accountability in budget setting. It also weakens ownership of budgets by operational managers, increasing the risk of overspends and reduced service discipline.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided
findings.quote: The Council was unable to evidence the involvement of budget holders in the development of the budget as the meetings between the budget holders and their linked finance business partner held as part of the budget setting and development process are not logged/recorded and actions coming out of these meeting are not tracked.

findings.headline: Efficiency programme inadequate: achieved only 0.3% of prior-year expenditure in cost savings.
findings.detail: The Council's formal efficiency programme for 2024/25 delivered only £143,300 in savings—just 0.3% of 2023/24 gross expenditure. There is no efficiency programme with a target as a percentage of prior-year spending, no formal schemes to achieve savings, and external benchmarking against other councils has not been performed due to capacity constraints.
findings.matters: Low efficiency delivery combined with lack of a structured savings programme indicates the Council is not systematically identifying cost reductions. This creates vulnerability to budget pressures and limits the Council's flexibility when grants are cut or demand increases.
findings.figures: Efficiency savings achieved: £143,300 (0.3% of 2023/24 gross expenditure)
findings.quote: While the Council has a Transformation Strategy which includes a key objective of 'Deliver high quality, value for money services that meet the needs of our customers' and a transformation objective of 'Identify and deliver efficiencies and cost reductions which we can re-invested into frontline services', there is not currently an efficiency programme which states a target as a percentage of the previous year's expenditure, and sets out the efficiency schemes by which the efficiency savings will be achieved.

findings.headline: Lack of segregation of duties in manual journal posting remains unresolved from prior year.
findings.detail: The auditors' prior-year recommendation about enforced segregation of duties in posting manual journal entries remains relevant and has not been addressed. This creates a risk that fraudulent or erroneous journals could be posted to the general ledger without detection.
findings.matters: Journal entry fraud is a key way councils conceal financial problems. This control gap, unresolved for at least two years, indicates management has deprioritized a known fraud risk.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided
findings.quote: The prior year recommendation regarding the lack of enforced segregation of duties in the posting of manual journal transactions remains relevant. There is a risk that fraudulent or erroneous journals are posted to the ledger which would lead to misstatements within the accounts.

findings.headline: Investment property contains an £82,000 unrecorded misstatement from a valuer's calculation error.
findings.detail: Auditors identified a calculation error by the valuer (Aspin & Company) resulting in an £82,000 understatement of one investment property's valuation. Management has not corrected this misstatement. While described as an isolated human error, the fact it was not corrected and testing was not extended raises questions about management's review controls.
findings.matters: Uncorrected misstatements are a sign of weak control environment and management override risk. Investment properties at £15.02m represent material balance sheet items.
findings.figures: Misstatement: £82,000; investment properties balance at 31 March 2024: £15.02m
findings.quote: We have identified a misstatement in the valuation of one of the Investment Properties selected for further testing. The misstatement arose due to a calculation error on the part of the valuer leading to an £82,000 difference in valuation. This misstatement has not been corrected by management.

findings.headline: Auditors have disclaimed their opinion on the 2024-25 financial statements due to pervasive audit evidence gaps.
findings.detail: KPMG cannot form an opinion on the financial statements as a whole because work on the split of usable and unusable reserves could not be completed by the statutory backstop date (27 February 2026), and this is considered pervasive to the Council's financial position. Multiple audit areas remain incomplete, including business rates income, land and buildings valuations, provisions, and comparative figures.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means audited accounts cannot be relied upon. This is a material governance failure and affects the credibility of reported reserves and financial position.
findings.figures: Statutory backstop deadline: 27 February 2026
findings.quote: Given our work to rebuild assurance is not complete and due to the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026, we have determined that there is insufficient time to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the split of useable and unusable reserves as at 31 March 2025 or 31 March 2024 ahead of the backstop, and, in our view, this is pervasive to the Council's financial position as at 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 3 2025/26 revenue and capital monitoring update report
findings.headline: Theatre revenue is underperforming, with Marine Hall admissions showing a £43,270 adverse variance driven by lower show bookings and a shift to profit-split arrangements with promoters
findings.detail: The theatre's business model has shifted from dry hire (guaranteed income) to split arrangements (revenue share), and show bookings through to year-end are lower than budget. This changes both the revenue stability and the profit expectation.
findings.matters: A lender concerned about revenue volatility needs to see whether income-generating assets are performing consistently; a shift from fixed-fee to variable arrangements and booking shortfalls suggest weaker control over theatre revenue.
findings.figures: Theatre admission income adverse variance: £43,270
findings.quote: Admission income is showing an adverse variance of £43,270 driven by projections on show bookings at Marine Hall through to the end of 2025/26, and a revised approach to bookings where shows are booked on a split basis with the promoter instead of a dry hire.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 3 2025/26 revenue and capital monitoring update report
findings.headline: Fleetwood Market service charge is being discounted to reflect ongoing heating challenges, indicating persistent operational problems with council-owned infrastructure
findings.detail: The building continues to have heating difficulties that are affecting its operational viability. The council is absorbing these costs by discounting the service charges, which appears to be an ongoing arrangement rather than a one-off issue.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether council assets are self-sustaining or dragging on the budget; persistent heating/operational problems at a revenue-generating asset suggest capital underinvestment or poor asset condition.
findings.figures: Service charge income adverse variance of £87,090
findings.quote: Fleetwood Market service charge continues to be discounted to reflect the ongoing challenges with heating the building.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 3 2025/26 revenue and capital monitoring update report
findings.headline: General fund balance is forecast to fall to £2.049m by March 2026, a reduction of £1.701m (45%) from the £3.750m held at end of 2024/25
findings.detail: The council is drawing down its general fund balance as planned, with the budget specifically approving a transfer of £1.7m from general fund balances. Whilst total usable reserves remain substantial at £39.019m forecast, the discretionary buffer (general fund balance) is shrinking.
findings.matters: A lender monitors whether a council is burning through its financial buffers to balance day-to-day spending; a falling general fund balance year-on-year signals reduced headroom for unplanned costs.
findings.figures: General fund balance 2024/25 year-end: £3.750m, Forecast 2026 year-end: £2.049m, Planned transfer: £1.700m
findings.quote: At the end of 2024/25... £3.750 million was held within the general fund balance... The budget plan to 31 March 2026 forecasts... £2.049 million is held within the general fund balance.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 3 2025/26 revenue and capital monitoring update report
findings.headline: Capital programme has expanded by 45% from the original approved budget, from £17.468m to £25.333m, with no explicit statement of funding source for the increase
findings.detail: The capital programme grew from the originally approved £17.468m to £21.514m at Q2, then further to £25.333m at Q3. Major additions include £3.844m for Wyre Beach Management Programme claims from the Environment Agency and £206,000 for acquisition of Garstang Swimming Pool. The paper does not detail what is funding this £7.865m expansion.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how significant capital growth is funded and whether it signals unplanned borrowing or reliance on uncertain external grants.
findings.quote: The original approved capital programme for 2025/26 was £17.468 million. This has increased from £21.514 million at Q2 to £25.333 million at Q3.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 3 2025/26 revenue and capital monitoring update report
findings.headline: Business rates collection rate has fallen 2.33 percentage points year-on-year, reflecting a wider trend across Lancashire
findings.detail: Current year business rates collection stands at 82.15%, down from 84.48% last year at the same point. The council notes this is part of a broader Lancashire trend, not isolated to Wyre. This is a material deterioration in a key income source (business rates represent 40% of the council's income share).
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in revenue stability; a 2.33% drop in collection rates suggests either economic conditions affecting businesses or administrative/collection issues that could worsen.
findings.figures: Current Year Collection Rate 82.15%, Last Year's Collection Rate 84.48%, Difference to last year -2.33%
findings.quote: business rates is lower than last year's Q3 figure and reflects the trend across Lancashire this year

findings.paper_title: Medium-Term Financial Plan mid-year update report
findings.headline: Material funding assumptions remain uncertain pending Fair Funding Review 2.0, EPR treatment, and food waste new burdens announcements
findings.detail: The MTFP relies on external consultant modelling of Fair Funding Review 2.0 impacts, which will not be confirmed until the Autumn Budget (26 Nov 2025) and LGFS (expected December). Extended Producer Responsibility funding of £995k is guaranteed only for 2025/26; its treatment in FFR2.0 is unknown. Food waste collection new burdens funding 'has yet to be announced' and there is risk it may already be included in the LG Futures modelling rather than being additional. The council acknowledges a 'cautious approach' is being taken pending clarity.
findings.matters: If government funding is less generous than modelled, or if new burdens fall short, the council's budget gaps could widen significantly, forcing either deeper savings or faster reserve depletion than forecast.
findings.quote: The new EPR (Extended Producer Responsibility) funding received in 2025/26 (guaranteed at £995,000 with the potential for a further increase) is not currently known to be included within the Fair Funding Review 2.0.

findings.paper_title: Medium-Term Financial Plan mid-year update report
findings.headline: Council exits Business Rates Pooling beyond 2025/26 due to scheme becoming 'less financially attractive and carry greater risk'
findings.detail: The MTFP removes the expectation of ongoing benefit from Business Rates Pooling beyond 2025/26. This reflects proposed revisions to the pooling scheme that the council assesses as disadvantageous. This removes a source of variable income and indicates an income headwind the council is unable to offset elsewhere.
findings.matters: Loss of expected pooling income places additional pressure on a council already requiring £2.75m+ annual reserve drawdowns and suggests treasury strategy assumptions are being progressively downgraded.
findings.figures: No specific amounts disclosed
findings.quote: The MTFP assumes no benefit from pooling will arise beyond 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Medium-Term Financial Plan mid-year update report
findings.headline: No funds set aside for Local Government Reorganisation despite possible council dissolution by April 2028
findings.detail: Wyre Council acknowledges it is 'entirely possible' it will cease to exist as a separate council beyond 1 April 2028 if Lancashire Local Government Reorganisation proceeds on current timescales. However, the MTFP ignores this risk and has set aside no funding. Precedent from Cumbria reorganisation suggests £1.5m per district would be required—potentially £1.5m of unbudgeted call on reserves.
findings.matters: If LGR proceeds, an unbudgeted £1.5m cost would materially worsen the council's reserve position and potentially force breach of balanced-budget duties, creating legal and financial risk for any lender.
findings.figures: £1.5m per district
findings.quote: No funds have been set aside for LGR but in the region of £1.5m per district was needed when Cumbria reorganised.

findings.paper_title: Medium-Term Financial Plan mid-year update report
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves will decline by £27.9m (73% reduction) from £38.2m to £10.3m by March 2030
findings.detail: The council will reduce earmarked reserves from £38.2m as at 1 April 2025 to £10.3m by 31 March 2030, whilst maintaining general balances at £2m. This dramatic drawdown reflects planned spending on Council Plan projects profiled to before April 2028 (coinciding with possible Local Government Reorganisation), leaving minimal reserves for unforeseen pressures by the end of the MTFP.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion materially reduces the council's financial resilience and flexibility to absorb shocks or fund discretionary activity, a key credit metric for lenders.
findings.figures: £38.2m reducing to £10.3m; General Balances held at £2.0m
findings.quote: Earmarked Reserves (excluding capital receipts of £2.6m as at 1 April 2025) will reduce from £38.2m down to £10.3m by 31 March 2030.

findings.paper_title: Medium-Term Financial Plan mid-year update report
findings.headline: Structural budget deficits require £2.75m–£4.1m annual reserve drawdown across the MTFP period
findings.detail: The updated MTFP shows Budget Equalisation Reserve use of £2.75m for 2026/27, £3.59m for 2027/28, £3.85m for 2028/29, and £4.09m for 2029/30. These figures are on an assumption that savings in each year are one-off. The position has improved slightly since March 2025, but the council cannot balance its budget from recurrent income and must draw down reserves every year.
findings.matters: Persistent structural deficits indicate the council's services are not sustainable from its core funding, and reserves will be depleted to fund operations rather than capital investment.
findings.quote: use of the Budget Equalisation Reserve/savings would be required of: • £2,753,697 for 2026/27 (was £3,300,000 in March 2025)

news_drafts.lead: Environmental remediation (lead removal) is a material liability. If Mount Pavilion requires lead replacement, other council buildings may have similar exposure, adding to future capital demands.
